# Exact tensor-affine polygonization with nonatomic curvature

This extends the tensor-independent part of
`candidate ec0876d0e4a0084f` from positive C2
curvature to uniformly mutually dominated nonatomic curvature measures. The
adaptive endpoint mesh is essential: no rate of decay of the curvature
measure near an endpoint is assumed. This is a local theorem, with explicit
cap guards and tensor independence; it does not assert global polygonization.

## 1. Statement and notation

Let P be a finite base in R^n. Let K_z, z in P, be positive planar convex
bodies satisfying every required Jensen Minkowski containment. Write h_z for
their support functions and R_z=h_z+h_z'' for their curvature measures.
Fix a closed normal interval I=[a,b] of length less than pi. Suppose:

1. On I the R_z are nonatomic. For a nonzero finite nonatomic measure nu
   and constants 0<c<=C<infinity, one has c nu<=R_z<=C nu for every z.
2. Both endpoints have inward one-sided accumulation of supp(nu).
3. For every prescribed cap and every fiber, the whole exposed boundary arc
   over I has one strict cap-membership sign, with a positive uniform margin.
4. Let B_z solve B_z''+B_z=0 with B_z(a)=h_z(a), B_z(b)=h_z(b), and put
   f_z=h_z-B_z in H_0^1(I). With e(z)=(1,z), the vectors e(z) tensor f_z
   are linearly independent.

Then, arbitrarily close to the given family, there is a compatible family
whose support functions are piecewise solutions of h''+h=0 on I and agree
with the original support functions outside I. Every individual fiber area,
and every prescribed cap area in every fiber, is exactly preserved.

The common curvature measures on I are consequently replaced by finitely
many curvature atoms. Zero-curvature endpoint portions can first be trimmed:
they already solve the homogeneous equation. If nu=0, no replacement is
needed. The theorem makes no assertion when tensor independence fails or
when the curvature measures are not uniformly mutually dominated.

For f,g in H_0^1(I), set

    Q(f,g)=integral_I (f'g'-fg).

This is positive definite and equivalent to the H_0^1 norm, by Poincare and
the assumption b-a<pi.

## 2. Common interpolation and exact projection error

For a finite common mesh a=t_0<...<t_s=b, let P_mesh f be the continuous
piecewise homogeneous interpolant taking the same values as f at all nodes.
On a cell [u,v] it is

    P_mesh f(theta)
      =[sin(v-theta) f(u)+sin(theta-u) f(v)]/sin(v-u).

This is Q-orthogonal projection onto the finite-dimensional subspace of
piecewise homogeneous functions in H_0^1(I). Indeed the interpolation error
vanishes at every node, and integration by parts against a homogeneous
function on each cell gives zero. These subspaces approximate H_0^1 as the
largest cell length tends to zero: first approximate by smooth functions,
whose displayed interpolants converge in H^1, and use the projection norm
bound. Thus P_mesh f -> f in H_0^1 for such meshes.

The interpolated support h_z^mesh=B_z+F_z, F_z=P_mesh f_z, is convex.
On each cell, h_z-h_z^mesh has zero endpoint values and positive
(D^2+1)-measure R_z, so it is nonpositive by the positive Dirichlet Green
kernel of -D^2-1. The jumps of the interpolant's derivative are nonnegative;
they also follow directly from the positive kernels described below.

Common interpolation preserves every Jensen inequality. Its two sine
coefficients are positive, so a nonnegative support gap at the nodes remains
nonnegative throughout each cell. Outside I nothing changes.

The area formula has a fixed endpoint term minus Q(f_z,f_z)/2. Therefore
the increase in fiber area under interpolation is exactly

    d_z=Q(f_z-F_z,f_z-F_z)/2.                         (1)

On a cell [u,v] of length delta<pi, the cell error energy is

    E_z[u,v]=integral integral G_uv(s,t) dR_z(s)dR_z(t),
    G_uv(s,t)=sin(s-u)sin(v-t)/sin(delta),   s<=t,

and symmetrically for t<=s. This follows by solving the zero-boundary
Dirichlet equation and then integrating Q(error)=-integral error dR_z.

## 3. Match the two small endpoint atoms

For the first cell [a,a+delta], define the reference outward endpoint atom

    eta_a(delta)
      = integral_(a,a+delta) sin(a+delta-s)/sin(delta) dnu(s). (2)

For a fiber, replace nu by R_z in this formula. To verify it, the exact
variation-of-constants identity is

    h_z(a+delta)=h_z(a)cos(delta)+h_z'(a)sin(delta)
                  +integral sin(a+delta-s)dR_z(s).

Thus (2) is the increase of the right derivative of the interpolant at a;
the outside left derivative remains unchanged. There is an analogous
positive endpoint atom eta_b(delta) at b, with sine weight sin(s-b+delta).

Both functions are continuous, tend to zero as delta decreases to zero,
and are strictly increasing for small positive delta. For example, at a
fixed s>a the derivative with respect to delta of the kernel in (2) is
sin(s-a)/sin(delta)^2>0, while the newly included upper endpoint has zero
kernel. The support accumulation hypothesis supplies positive mass inside
every sufficiently small cell. Continuity follows by dominated convergence,
using nonatomicity at the moving upper endpoint. The right endpoint is the
same after reversing the interval.

Choose a sequence eta decreasing to zero, and choose first and last cell
lengths delta_a,delta_b so that their reference endpoint atoms both equal
eta. Both lengths tend to zero. Every fiber endpoint atom is then at least
c eta by mutual domination.

The reference Green energy of the first cell obeys

    E_nu[a,a+delta] <= 2 delta nu([a,a+delta]) eta_a(delta).  (3)

Indeed on the half-square s<=t, sin(s-a)<=delta, and the remaining kernel
factor is exactly the weight defining eta_a at t. Integrating and doubling
proves (3). The second endpoint has the analogous estimate. Since the
endpoint lengths tend to zero, their errors are o(eta). Moreover
E_z<=C^2 E_nu, so this is uniform over the finite fiber family.

After fixing these two endpoint cells, refine all interior cells until
their combined errors for every fiber are at most eta^2, and until their
maximum length tends to zero. This is possible by the projection convergence
on the remaining closed interval, or separately on any preliminary finite
interior partition. The resulting whole-mesh errors satisfy

    max_z d_z=o(eta).                                     (4)

No uniform density or algebraic mesh-error rate has been used.

## 4. Restore every area by an affine-in-base correction

Define the tensor Gram matrix

    A_zw=(e(z).e(w)) Q(F_z,F_w).

By tensor independence and H^1 convergence, A is positive definite for
all sufficiently fine meshes, with uniformly bounded inverse. Seek

    Psi_z=sum_w xi_w (e(z).e(w)) F_w.

The map z -> Psi_z is affine, so adding it cancels exactly from every
Jensen support difference, including at changing or dense contact sets.

The area decrease after this addition is exactly

    (A xi)_z+q_z(xi),       q_z(xi)=Q(Psi_z,Psi_z)/2.

Solve A xi+q(xi)=d. The coefficients of q are uniformly bounded, as are
A inverse and the norms of all F_z. Thus the map

    xi -> A^(-1)(d-q(xi))

is a contraction on a ball of radius a fixed constant times ||d|| for
sufficiently small ||d||. For completeness, choose the constant greater
than twice the uniform inverse bound. The quadratic bound on q makes the
map preserve that ball when ||d|| is small, and its Lipschitz constant
there is O(||d||)<1. Its unique fixed point satisfies

    ||xi||=O(||d||)=o(eta).                               (5)

Consequently all fiber areas are restored exactly.

## 5. Convexity after correction, including the small endpoint atoms

At an interior mesh node, the interpolant's curvature atom is the sum of
two positive-kernel integrals of R_z over its neighboring cells. This is
the derivative-jump version of (2). Mutual domination therefore gives,
uniformly over every mesh node and every pair of fibers,

    atom_w <= (C/c) atom_z.                               (6)

The homogeneous function B_w has no interior curvature, so these are also
the interior curvature atoms of F_w. The correction to fiber z's atom is
bounded in absolute value by a fixed constant times ||xi|| atom_z, using
(6) and the finitely many coefficients e(z).e(w). It cannot make the atom
negative once ||xi|| is sufficiently small. If an atom is zero, every
correction atom at that node is zero as well.

At a or b the derivative jumps of the zero-extended F_w are uniformly
bounded. One way to see this is the endpoint formula above, the bounded
first derivatives of h_w, and the fixed bounded derivatives of B_w.
Hence the endpoint correction atom is O(||xi||)=o(eta), whereas the
interpolant's positive endpoint atom is at least c eta. Those atoms remain
nonnegative too. Outside I the support and curvature measures are unchanged.
Thus the corrected functions are support functions of convex bodies.

## 6. Exact cap preservation and scope

Nonatomic curvature makes h_z continuously differentiable on I. The common
interpolants converge uniformly in support and one-sided boundary
derivatives: this follows either from the variation-of-constants formula,
since the maximum curvature mass of a shrinking cell tends to zero, or
from uniform continuity of h_z'. The corrections and their piecewise
derivatives tend uniformly to zero as well. Thus every changed boundary
piece, including the short endpoint facets, remains in its original strict
cap-membership region. Outside these pieces the boundaries are unchanged.

For a fixed fiber and prescribed cap, its area change is therefore either
zero (if the changed arc lies outside the cap) or precisely its whole area
change (if the arc lies inside). The latter is zero by the area restoration.
This can also be read from the oriented boundary area integral, splitting
the boundary at the unchanged endpoints and the fixed cap intersection
points. Every prescribed cap area is exactly preserved.

The construction preserves arbitrary Jensen contact patterns because the
interpolation is positive and the correction is affine in the base. It
requires common nonatomic domination and tensor independence, and the
changed arcs must have separated cap memberships. It does not remove any
of these hypotheses by a limiting assertion.

## 7. The rank-one exception and families of at most three fibers

There is also an exact repair if f_z=c_z f with c_z>0 and
nu=f''+f nonzero and nonatomic. This includes the only tensor-rank failure
for three collinear indices: a tensor dependence gives two linear equations
forcing the three residuals to be proportional. Each residual is strictly
negative in the interval interior by the positive Dirichlet Green kernel,
so the proportionality constants are positive. For affinely independent
indices the tensor vectors are automatically independent.

Every Jensen gap now has the form g=D+kappa f>=0, D''+D=0. If kappa is
nonzero, BV locality on {g=0} gives

    (g''+g)^c restricted to {g=0}=0,

and therefore nu({g=0})=0. The proof of this locality statement is in
`candidate 181e74b2f3c435dc`; it uses g>=0,
g' in BV, and the diffuse derivative locality on a level set. If kappa=0,
a nonzero homogeneous nonnegative gap has no interior zero; an interior
zero has zero derivative and forces the homogeneous solution to vanish.
An identity gap necessarily has D=kappa=0, since nu is nonzero.

There are only finitely many necessary Jensen gaps. Hence there is a
compact interval J inside I with nu(J)>0 and with every nonidentity gap
uniformly positive on J. Choose a nonzero source nu'<=nu supported compactly
inside J. There is a bounded signed density psi with the two sine/cosine
moments zero such that its compact Green potential phi satisfies

    phi''+phi=psi nu',       Q(f,phi)=-integral phi dnu !=0. (7)

Here is an exact justification of the nonzero pairing, rather than a
genericity assertion. If every such compact potential had zero pairing,
the singular-support potential-locality lemma, with source nu' and target
measure nu, would give nu restricted to supp(nu') equal to zero. This
contradicts 0<nu'(J)<=nu(supp(nu')). Change the sign of phi so that the
pairing in (7) is positive.

Use any sufficiently fine common mesh, F=P_mesh f and Phi=P_mesh phi.
The latter vanishes on neighborhoods of a and b. Put

    A=Q(F,Phi)>0, B=Q(Phi,Phi)>0, E=Q(f-F,f-F),
    xi=E/[A+sqrt(A^2+B E)].

Then 2A xi+B xi^2=E and xi tends to zero. Thus F+xi Phi has exactly the
same Q norm as f, and B_z+c_z(F+xi Phi) restores every fiber area exactly.
The correction is supported in the fixed strict-gap guard J. Identity
gaps are unchanged, and all other gaps remain nonnegative for small xi.

At every interior mesh node, the curvature atom of Phi is a positive-kernel
integral of psi nu', so its absolute value is at most ||psi||_infinity
times the corresponding atom of the interpolated nu. Therefore the small
scalar correction preserves convexity, including zero atoms. There are no
endpoint corrections at a,b at all. The cap argument of Section 6 applies.

Consequently the local theorem holds for at most three positive fibers
under its common nonatomic domination and cap-guard hypotheses, without
requiring tensor independence. For three collinear fibers use this section
in the rank-one case; otherwise use Sections 1--6. For three affinely
independent fibers tensor independence is automatic. This does not remove
the common domination or cap-guard hypotheses.
